Q5115.L1t: Lactate is produced in skeletal muscle when pyruvate is converted to lactate by lactate dehydrogenase, regenerating NAD+.
Q5115.L2t: During exercise, the rate of glycolysis and the rate of pyruvate production can exceed the rate at which mitochondria oxidise pyruvate, so some pyruvate is diverted to lactate.
Q5115.L3t: At the onset of exercise, glycolytic flux rises rapidly while oxidative metabolism takes time to catch up, so pyruvate and NADH accumulate and pyruvate is reduced to lactate.
Q5115.L4t: Muscle lactate production rises when glycolysis is switched on at the start of exercise.
Q5115.L2f: Lactate dehydrogenase converts lactate to acetyl-CoA directly inside muscle cells, which is why it is found mainly in mitochondria.
Q5115.L3f: Lactate is formed from glucose breakdown only when the pathway cannot generate pyruvate, so blocking pyruvate formation is what pushes the muscle to make lactate.
Q5115.L4f: Muscle lactate production increases when pyruvate cannot be formed from glucose breakdown.

Q8288.L1t: Roger Williams was a 17th-century English Protestant minister who founded Rhode Island and argued for separating church and state.
Q8288.L2t: Puritans left England to practise their own religion freely, and in Massachusetts Bay they kept church membership and civil privileges tied to their own congregations, which Williams criticised.
Q8288.L3t: The passage criticises the civil state for imposing religion, and Williams was banished from Massachusetts because the Puritan colony itself did not tolerate dissenting beliefs and enforced its own orthodoxy.
Q8288.L4t: The Puritans meant religious freedom to cover themselves alone, not other groups.
Q8288.L2f: Puritan Massachusetts Bay was founded as a colony with a legally established policy of welcoming every religious group, and Williams was invited there as a guest preacher.
Q8288.L3f: Puritan colonial law granted religious liberty to every Christian denomination, including Catholics and Quakers, and banished only non-Christians.
Q8288.L4f: The Puritans believed religious freedom should be extended to all Christians.

Q5932.L1t: Intermittent high-intensity exercise such as football or sprint games draws heavily on both muscle glycogen and blood glucose as fuel.
Q5932.L2t: During prolonged intermittent high-intensity exercise, plasma adrenaline and other counter-regulatory hormones are elevated, and the liver supplies glucose to the blood.
Q5932.L3t: Intense bursts raise catecholamines, which stimulate hepatic glucose output beyond the rate at which working muscle takes glucose up, and muscle glycogen supplies much of the fuel.
Q5932.L4t: Blood glucose frequently rises by about 1 to 3 mM over this kind of exercise.
Q5932.L2f: Blood glucose in intermittent high-intensity exercise is regulated mainly by rising insulin secretion, which drives glucose from the blood into muscle throughout the session.
Q5932.L3f: In intermittent high-intensity exercise lasting 80-90 minutes, liver glycogen is exhausted and muscle uptake outstrips hepatic output, so blood glucose steadily declines.
Q5932.L4f: Blood glucose falls to hypoglycaemic levels during 80-90 minutes of intermittent high-intensity exercise.
